stories.headline: Cyclone Arnab: APEPDCL opens 41 control rooms, keeps 4,056 workers ready to restore power
stories.title: Cyclone Arnab: APEPDCL opens 41 control rooms, keeps 4,056 workers ready to restore power
stories.summary: People in Kakinada, East Godavari and Konaseema, the districts likely to bear the brunt, can report power problems on helpline 1912
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Andhra Pradesh Eastern Power Distribution Company Limited (APEPDCL) has stepped up its preparedness for Cyclone Arnab and is concentrating on Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, Godavari and Kakinada districts, towards which the storm is expected to make landfall.

Following the India Meteorological Department (IMD)’s warning about Cyclone Arnab over the east-central and adjoining south-east Bay of Bengal, the utility has mobilised personnel, machinery and electrical materials to minimise disruptions and speed up power restoration in affected areas.
APEPDCL has opened 30 divisional control rooms, in addition to 11 circle-level control rooms, to monitor the situation and coordinate emergency response.
Kakinada and East Godavari have three divisional control rooms each, and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema has two.
A separate cell has been established at the corporate office to coordinate manpower deployment round the clock under the supervision of the Chief General Manager (Operations and Customer Service).
APEPDCL CMD I. Prudhvi Tej held a teleconference with senior engineering officials to review cyclone preparedness.
The utility has also sought 150 teams of 10 personnel each from the Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APSPDCL) and requested additional materials from it.
The utility has arranged 394 contractor teams comprising 4,056 personnel for emergency response and restoration work.
The available resources include 211 diesel generator sets, 273 pole-drilling machines, 517 power saws and 318 earth movers and cranes.
A fleet of 366 departmental and private vehicles has been listed to transport personnel and materials to affected locations.
Another 100 mobile handsets have been arranged for communication during emergency operations.
APEPDCL said it had stocks of conductors, cables, distribution transformers and electric poles as of October 25.

The IMD expects the storm to grow stronger by Monday midnight and stronger still on Tuesday.

stories.headline: Odisha bans fishing, tourist entry in 6 districts amid cyclone alert
stories.title: Odisha bans fishing, tourist entry in 6 districts amid cyclone alert
stories.summary: The government has mobilised its resources in Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Malkangiri, Koraput and Nabarangpur, the identified vulnerable districts of the southern region
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Odisha government has prohibited fishing activities in the sea and banned entry of tourists in the hills, waterfalls and dams in six districts as it has stepped up precautionary measures in view of a cyclonic storm that is likely to make landfall in neighbouring Andhra Pradesh within 48 hours, officials said on Monday (October 26, 2026).

The government has mobilised its resources in Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Malkangiri, Koraput and Nabarangpur, the identified vulnerable districts of the southern region, while Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi deputed eight ministers at separate places to monitor pre-cyclone activities, they said.

Rescue teams, comprising personnel of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF), the Fire and Emergency Services, and the police, have been pre-positioned in vulnerable areas, the officials said.
The cyclonic storm, 'Arnab', is likely to make landfall along the neighbouring Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday (October 28, 2026), according to an IMD forecast.

The India Meteorological Department, in its bulletin on Monday (October 26, 2026) morning, said the deep depression over the Bay of Bengal moved nearly westwards with a speed of 15 kmph during the past six hours and intensified into a cyclonic storm.

“It is very likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify further into a severe cyclonic storm over west-central Bay of Bengal by midnight of October 26 and into a very severe cyclonic storm over the same region on October 27,” it said.

Odisha’s Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari said, "Although the system is expected to cross the Andhra Pradesh coast, the Odisha government would take no chances and remain fully prepared to deal with any eventuality."
After landfall, the weather system is projected to move to certain areas within Odisha's territory.
The State government is "fully prepared to tackle the situation", and therefore there is no reason to panic, the Minister said.

"Fishing activities in the sea have been completely prohibited, while tourist entry into hills, waterfalls, dams, and scenic destinations across the vulnerable six districts has also been banned," he said.
In view of inclement weather conditions, schools, colleges, and Anganwadi centres in these districts will remain closed on October 28 and 29.
The government has cancelled leave of its employees in the identified districts, and control rooms have been opened to coordinate relief and rescue operations, the Minister said.

stories.headline: Cyclone Arnab may take heavy rain regime away from South Peninsula
stories.title: Cyclone Arnab may take heavy rain regime away from South Peninsula
stories.summary: The building very severe cyclone is expected to track north-northeastwards, dragging a sprawling rain across large swathes eastern and central India, and away from most of the South Peninsula
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Sunday’s depression gathered steam at accelerated pace overnight on Monday and intensified twice over to become cycloneArnab, the first of this north-east monsoon, over the east-central and adjoining south-east Bay.
Moving at a brisk 15 km/hr early on Monday, the system is expected to intensify further into a very severe cyclone, putting the Andhra Pradesh coast squarely in the firing line.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) located the storm about 650 km east-south-east of Visakhapatnam; 730 km east-south-east of Kakinada; 830 km east of Machilipatnam; and 910 km east of Bapatla, all in Andhra Pradesh.
The cyclone is forecast to barrel west-north-west, strengthen into a severe cyclone over the west-central Bay by midnight and a very severe cyclonic storm over the same region on Tuesday.

It is then expected to swing north-westwards and cross the Andhra Pradesh-Yanam coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam by Wednesday morning, packing maximum sustained winds of 115-125 km/hr, gusting to 140 km/hr.
The cyclone’s landfall, however, will be far from the end of the story.
Although it will lose some punch after moving ashore, Arnab is expected to track north-north-eastwards, dragging a sprawling rain across large swathes of eastern and central India.

Extremely heavy to very heavy rainfall, with heavy spells in several areas, is forecast across Odisha, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal, Vidarbha, east Madhya Pradesh and east Uttar Pradesh over the three to four days beginning Wednesday.
The unfolding scenario could therefore shift the rain action away from much of the South Peninsula.

The heavy-rain regime that has held sway over large parts of Tamil Nadu and adjoining South Peninsula, barring southern Tamil Nadu and Kerala, may give way to Arnab and its northward march into the eastern farming heartland of the country and farther east, with its reach extending towards east Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
Chennai remained partly cloudy at 10 am, and may continue to remain same through the day today (Monday).
The sheer geographical spread of the rainfall threat reflects the system’s expected staying power.

stories.headline: Over 61,000 Form-7 applications filed by election officials in Karnataka, none cites reason
stories.title: Over 61,000 Form-7 applications filed by election officials in Karnataka, none cites reason
stories.summary: Officials say they were instructed to file Form-7 applications for shifted, duplicate, underage, deceased and non-citizen voters, but auto-generated forms left the reason blank
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: At least 61,059 Form-7 applications seeking the deletion of names from Karnataka’s electoral rolls were filed by election officials themselves, with not a single application mentioning a reason for the deletion, a mandatory requirement under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) and Assistant Electoral Registration.

Officers (AEROs), listed as the objectors in these applications, said the system “auto-generated” the forms with their digital signatures when voters could not be reached during hearings on notices issued for no mapping or logical discrepancies, and the voters were therefore marked as “ineligible”.
This meant the same election machinery was raising objections to voters’ names and deciding on whether they should remain on the rolls.
Under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 an objection that is not filed in the prescribed manner, including stating the reason, is liable to be rejected.
The officials said they had been instructed to file Form-7 applications if a voter had shifted, had a duplicate entry elsewhere, was underage, had died, or was not an Indian citizen.
But as the forms were auto-generated, the reason for seeking deletion was left blank.
With no reason recorded, neither the voter nor anyone examining the electoral roll can establish why a particular name was marked for deletion or verify whether the removal was justified.

Moreover, these categories of voters (ASDDO or Absent, Shifted, Duplicate, Dead and Others) had already been checked during the enumeration phase of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which led to more than 1.07 crore names being deleted from Karnataka’s draft electoral roll.
Most deletions were on the grounds of voters having permanently shifted, followed by those marked as absent.
The number of Form-7 applications filed by election officials rose sharply after the claims and objections period ended on September 23, 2026.
Between August 24 and September 23, only 192 such applications were received.

He also cautioned that any resolution passed would become binding immediately.

“Instead of coming to this Court, we could have resolved it.
Why waste the valuable time of this Court?” Rai said, adding that the executive committee preferred consulting members before forming an opinion.
CJI Surya Kant clarified that the court-appointed committee's proposals aim to strengthen genuine practitioners rather than curtail their rights.
“Those who are genuinely regular visitors to the Supreme Court, having an interest in the Bar, the institution and the system, we want to strengthen their hands.

stories.headline: China’s Solar Technology Curbs: A Global Warning That Could Make the Energy Transition More Expensive
stories.title: China’s Solar Technology Curbs: A Global Warning That Could Make the Energy Transition More Expensive
stories.summary: China’s solar industry helped transform renewable energy from an increasingly competitive alternative into one of the cheapest sources of new electricity generation worldwide. But Beijing’s latest proposal to restrict exports of selected solar manufacturing technologies raises a difficult question: does China want the world to go solar—or does it want to retain control over the industry that makes solar possible? On October 16, China proposed adding 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies to its export-control framework. The measures include proposed prohibitions on certain technologies used to manufacture advanced perovskite and tandem cells, ultra-thin silicon wafers and particular polysilicon production systems. Other technologies, including selected TOPCon, heterojunction and back-contact cell manufacturing processes, would face restrictions rather than outright prohibitions. The proposal is part of a broader revision covering 40 technologies across sectors including solar energy, artificial intelligence and biomedicine. China has cited national security and the protection of strategic technologies as reasons for the proposed measures. The consultation process runs until November 15, 2026. The distinction matters: the proposal does not amount to a blanket ban on exporting finished solar modules. Its potential significance lies further upstream—in the equipment-related know-how, production processes and technical expertise that countries need to build their own competitive manufacturing capabilities. If implemented, the restrictions could complicate the efforts of countries that are trying to reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing even as they continue to depend on Chinese technology to establish their own factories. Europe: Strategic independence could come at a premium Europe may be among the most uncomfortable cases. The European Union wants to rebuild its clean-technology manufacturing base, diversify supply chains and reduce strategic dependence on China. Yet its solar industry remains heavily reliant on Chinese products and manufacturing capabilities. The cost of alternatives is already a concern. S&P Global reported in August 2026 that European efforts to diversify solar supply chains faced substantial cost hurdles. One supplier indicated that solar modules sourced from Turkey could cost roughly twice as much as comparable Chinese supply, while European manufacturing continues to struggle with scale and competitiveness. Indian manufacturers offer another possible source of supply, but they are not necessarily a low-cost substitute. S&P Global's reporting found that Indian TOPCon utility-scale module prices had maintained a premium of at least $0.14 per watt over Chinese equivalents on a free-on-board basis during 2026. These figures concern alternative module supply, not the direct cost of replacing restricted manufacturing technologies. Nevertheless, they illustrate the price Europe may pay when it prioritises supply-chain resilience over the cheapest available imports. The proposed Chinese controls could add another complication. If European companies cannot readily obtain selected advanced manufacturing processes or associated equipment technologies from China, developing domestic capacity may become slower and more expensive. Existing European capabilities in research, specialised machinery and engineering could help, but they cannot necessarily replace China's scale overnight. For European policymakers, the response may have to be selective rather than absolute: support strategically important manufacturing stages, secure alternative technology partnerships, encourage long-term purchasing agreements and accept a price premium where the security benefits justify it. Attempting to reproduce the entire Chinese supply chain domestically would be expensive. But continuing to rely almost entirely on a single source would leave Europe exposed to future policy changes. India: An opportunity with an upstream vulnerability India's predicament is different. It has built substantial solar module manufacturing capacity and is expanding cell production, while seeking to deepen its presence in wafers, ingots and polysilicon. The proposed controls could complicate this transition, particularly where new factories depend on Chinese manufacturing equipment, process knowledge or technical assistance. Restrictions affecting advanced cell technologies could also make it harder for Indian companies to move quickly into the next generation of high-efficiency products. There is, however, an opportunity. If technology access becomes less predictable, Indian manufacturers and policymakers have a stronger incentive to invest in domestic research, develop engineering expertise and build alternative partnerships with equipment suppliers and research institutions in Japan, South Korea, Europe and elsewhere. India could also benefit if global manufacturers seek alternative production locations. But that opportunity is not automatic: factories require competitive equipment, skilled personnel, reliable infrastructure, predictable policy and customers willing to pay for products made outside China. New Delhi will need to distinguish between capacity expansion and genuine technological independence. A large module factory that depends on imported cells and externally controlled production know-how offers less strategic autonomy than an integrated supply chain with domestic engineering capabilities. The United States: Industrial policy meets technology access The United States has invested heavily in domestic clean-energy manufacturing and sought to diversify away from Chinese supply chains. The proposed restrictions could complicate selected expansion plans that rely on Chinese technologies, including advanced manufacturing processes. For US companies, alternative equipment suppliers, domestic research and development, licensing arrangements where available, and partnerships with manufacturers in allied economies could offer routes forward. But these alternatives may require more capital, additional time and greater technical effort. The challenge is particularly acute in emerging technologies. A country may be able to establish a conventional solar module factory without possessing the know-how required to manufacture next-generation tandem cells at scale. Restrictions on those processes could widen the gap between countries that control advanced manufacturing technology and those that merely assemble products. At the same time, the US could view the proposal as further justification for investing in domestic capabilities. Whether that investment produces globally competitive manufacturing or simply more expensive capacity will depend on execution and sustained demand. article_sentences: HDFC Bank shares fell 0.71 per cent to ₹687.90 on the NSE by 12.15 pm Monday, extending the stock’s week-long slide as new chief executive Anup Bagchi formally assumed office.
Sellers dominated trade, accounting for 55.32 per cent of total quantity against buyers at 44.68 per cent, with traded volume reaching 115.52 lakh shares worth ₹797.01 crore.
The stock now sits just ₹6 above its 52-week low of ₹681.90, having shed nearly 31 per cent year-to-date against the Nifty 50’s 13.59 per cent decline over the same period.
The P/E ratio has compressed to 13.34, with the adjusted figure at 13.15.
Bagchi inherits a bank under strain on multiple fronts.
An internal probe into alleged disclosure of confidential information by two senior executives remains active and unresolved.
Deputy Managing Director Kaizad Bharucha is scheduled to exit by December, compounding the leadership transition.
Sashidhar Jagdishan, whom Bagchi succeeds, steps down after six years.
Broader banking sector pressure added to the headwinds.
Bank Nifty opened below its previous close near 54,250, breaking below the 54,000 mark.
The RSI has slipped into the mid-30s, signalling sustained selling momentum.
Immediate support is seen at 53,800–53,700, while resistance lies at 54,300–54,400.
